text: 1,275 takedown orders a day. One every 68 seconds. No notice. No hearing. That’s not law and order but that is a mute button on public anger. When criticism vanishes faster than it can be posted, the internet stops being a public square and becomes a government-controlled feed.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

The Delhi High Court on Tuesday (September 29, 2026) directed social media platforms to remove several fake profiles, channels and deepfake videos allegedly misusing the name, image and identity of Drishti IAS founder Vikas Divyakirti.

🐾 MORNING FETCH — OCTOBER 3

Last night we published a developer who closed his own eighteen-hour gap. Overnight the same developer published something harder: his verifier had been wrong, in a way that reported truncated AI answers as verified, and he said so in the release notes.

1/ A verifier that said "verified" when it should not have. Fixed, disclosed, and filed in the standards repo six hours later

At 19:02Z BruceBlue shipped TapeAPI 1.5, and the headline is not a feature. Versions 1.0.0 through 1.4.0 could, under particular chunking, report a truncated or content-injected OpenAI Chat or Responses stream as verified. In 1.5.0 strict mode cuts the stream at its end, and an unfinished event or a hidden character at the start of a line fails closed. The receipt hash and the spec are unchanged. His own instruction: if you verify streamed receipts, please upgrade.

Two more holes closed in the same release. Usage verification can no longer be switched off by one line inside a receipt. And hidden instructions in MCP tool descriptions — invisible characters — are now refused outright.

He is explicit about how the bugs were found and what that is worth: several rounds of adversarial review, AI-assisted, not a third-party audit. And at the end of the post, twice: still not audited by a third party. No token. Just open source.

Now the part a reader can check, because it did not stay on X. At 01:16:19Z and 01:16:20Z — six hours and fourteen minutes after the post — the same author pushed d282218 to PR #26 and c9995d6 to PR #16 in the TapeOut standards repository, each naming release v1.5.0 at commit d991f5e, and each opening with a request the editors cannot skim past: these requirements were not part of the format check you did on October 1, so please look again before merging.

What #26 now says, in section numbers. The end of a stream is a point in the bytes (§6.1), so bytes after that point are covered by no receipt and a strict client stops passing the stream on (§9.2). A stream whose bytes close while an event is unfinished is discarded by the rules, but some clients dispatch it when the body ends, so the client check fails closed (§5.2, §9.3 item 8). A line starting with U+FEFF anywhere but the very start is an ambiguous line — and the reason it is in the spec at all is that the official OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, tested, strip a byte order mark from every line and read it as a data line. Test material: 22 streams of three formats, 0 mismatches, plus a comparison against the reference scanner on 40,000 random streams.

What #16 now says. The earlier text asked clients to flag Unicode category Cf and Cc characters, and that is not enough: 256 variation selectors can spell any text one byte at a time, and U+2800 and U+1D159 look blank too. "Hidden code point" is now defined by Unicode 17.0 properties, with one exception — a single U+FE0E or U+FE0F directly after an Emoji. The Security Considerations say what the rule does not cover, including that Persian and Hindi texts using U+200C or U+200D get refused as well. 38 tool lists tested, 5 allowed, 33 refused, 0 mismatches.

2/ The oldest unanswered drafts got reviewed. Not by an editor

Yesterday we counted twelve branches in the standards repository with no editor comment, and said the four jeffwang996 Issues had waited more than 33 hours. Two of them have now been answered — by ronesync, the contributor whose own draft the editors numbered TAP-20.

Issue #29 waited 1 day 11h 23m. Issue #30 waited 1 day 12h 31m. Neither reply is a courtesy.

Both start with the question the author actually asked — separate profile, or amendment to TAP-10? — and answer it with the test from TAP-01 §3: if only clients that opt in must follow it, it is an Application TAP; if every compliant shell must, it is a change to TAP-10 itself, which means a pull request touching only TAP-10.md and approved by that document's authors. Then both do something an editor has not done in this repository yet: check the author's citations. Quoting #30: "I checked the TAP-10 and TAP-11 references in the issue and in both comments against the text, and they are accurate." Followed by the list — one pinned block per open site, per-file length and SHA-256 checks, what fileInfo returns, what putFile and appendChunk do.

And buried in that list, a fact that changes what the draft has to say: TAP-10 Appendix A allows those writes from an operator set with setOperator, not only from the holder. In ronesync's words, that matters for any statement about who a manifest is attributable to.

The reviews also find the walls. The release manifest cannot live at /sw.js or under /.tape/, because TAP-10 §8.8 reserves both for gateways. TAP-10 §7.1 already caps one file at 8,400,000 bytes and lets a client stop listing after 5,000 paths, so a manifest's own budgets have to relate to those. And on #29: PR #8 has since merged as TAP-11, so the issue's "builds on" reference is already out of date.

Meanwhile the editors. TheCYPER's last comment anywhere in the repository is still 18:41:33Z on October 1 — 1 day 8h 59m of silence at our reading. No commit has landed on main since the #37 merge at 09:41:39Z yesterday. Sixth day with 0 submitted reviews, 0 review comments, no label except [idea], no assignee, no requested reviewer. The external cryptographic reviewer for #12 and #20 still has not appeared; #20, #28, #33 and #34 have zero comments of any kind.

One new branch, opened at 18:38:33Z: Issue #38, payment vouchers for container services, by the TapeAPI author. It is the most self-limiting proposal in the repository. It asks for a discussion rather than a draft, so that TapeOut is not handed a second payment standard. It says the escrow contract is implemented and tested but not deployed and not audited, and will not be deployed before an independent audit. It then says the consequence out loud: TAP-01 §5 lets a TAP that depends on an upgradeable contract become Final only after that contract is sealed, so this draft would stay a Draft for a long time. And it asks the editors four direct questions, including whether TapeOut plans its own payment mechanism this should align with.

Counters: open branches 29 → 30, which is #38 arriving. Stars 8, forks 7 — unchanged, so yesterday's first-ever decline did not continue.

Why it matters: a standards process is working when people who are not in charge start doing the careful work anyway. Two of the four oldest ignored Issues got the kind of reply that tells an author exactly what to write next, and the reviewer had no authority to send it.

The sharpest community line of the night came from the host of that podcast, answering a listener at 20:59. The point was never canonisation, he wrote, it is whether the system can run without one person. Rules written into contracts make the system independent of the founder; a laid-out tool chain makes builders independent of him. Rules written down first is the harder and rarer of the two — because if the rules stay in one person's hands, however smooth the tools, builders have no confidence.

Which sits oddly well next to our own reading. https://t.co/PLbwJD16VL's admin surface still reads the BEM mining contract as sealed with no owner, and the TapeHub launchpad's 249 projects as upgradeable by a single wallet, 0x8446…fc51, with the circuit and transistor beacons held behind a 3-of-5 Safe. Official accounts, eleven posts, and two of them are mechanism rather than slogan. @BEMGoGoGo on challenge: if a verified Circuit is wrong, anyone can submit a Counterexample Vector against it, no stake required — verification is not a one-time stamp, it stays open to proof. And on precedence: BEM is Optimal First, not First To Solve. For each Task the lowest valid Design Cost holds the Optimal Slot; if a better Design arrives, the earlier Builder keeps the Burned Work but loses the Design Premium; submit a Design Commitment before Tape Out and it protects your slot from copy-based front running. Plus the one-liner: one Circuit today is a building block tomorrow, because a completed Circuit can be used as a Black Box in the next Design.

@Hashport01 shipped six posts and every one is an answer to a real support ticket. A wallet can check every file the page loaded against its registered hash before signing, and if they do not match, signing should not happen. Bytes written on chain cannot be deleted, so before you drop in dist, check once more for private keys, API keys, .env files and database passwords. Works locally but 404 on chain is usually a path mismatch, because the console does not rewrite your references. A single file caps at 8.4 MB, so split bundles, compress what compresses, and link images and video externally. On Cloudflare, point the CNAME at the gateway and put the container address in the TXT, both set to DNS only. And at 18:03, four words: build first, explain later.

@spongemochi stopped posting aphorisms and shipped the thing. At 17:16, 168 · 一路发 on X Layer: write one sentence, the capsule opens on its due date, and right or wrong it stays on chain forever. His own framing is better than a pitch — not a prophecy archive, but credit growing out of a record, where every judgement a person or an Agent makes becomes a voucher for allocating resources later. Entered in the TapeOut Genesis Transistor Hackathon. He also has the matching draft in the standards repository, Issue #5 and PR #6, sealed commitments and verdicts over TapeSend, open since September 30.

Its BEM price reads $35.76 against the burn board's $36.24 at nearly the same minute, which is two reads of one pool, not two prices.

Nobody in this yard keeps hours. @ywweb3 was answering replies at 03:26 and explained why: could not sleep. @BruceBlue surfaced at 02:37 with "just woke up", and two minutes earlier had answered a stranger about agent wrappers with the only line that matters in that argument — the real constraint is keeping the wrapper cheaper than the call itself. A good night in the yard: one developer said his own tool had been wrong, a reviewer with no badge did the editors' work, and the burn board held perfectly still. Three different kinds of honest. 🐾

KNOWN FACTS ABOUT THE WEAPONIZED VETERAN AFFAIRS @DeptVetAffairs @codeofvets @nicksortor @nickshirleyy @POTUS @SecWar @SecScottBessent 
A false no-show is one tool. These are the others that show up in the record, in OIG audits, and in claim files. Some are policy. Some are bad data that the agency then treats as fact. The effect on the veteran is the same.
The chart is written against him. “Veteran refused,” “noncompliant,” “no acute distress,” and “ambulating without difficulty” get entered when he was in pain, unstable, or never examined the way the note says. A later rater, nurse, or judge reads that note as the truth. Amendment requests go to the same facility. Privacy officers deny them. The false note stays, and every new decision cites it.
Scheduling numbers are protected, not the veteran. OIG has repeatedly found clinic cancellations entered as “canceled by patient,” hidden wait lists, and off-books tracking. The computer shows a short wait. The veteran waits months. A no-show or a patient-cancel code keeps the miss off the facility’s access report.
Consults die on a timer. Miss the appointment, miss the callback, or miss a letter, and staff can discontinue the consult without a doctor reviewing it. Community-care consults are worse. In the first quarter of fiscal 2025, OIG found about 45 percent of VA consults and 60 percent of community-care consults missed the scheduling standard, and about half of both missed the standard for actually being seen. Eligible veterans are also scheduled inside VA with no record they were told they could go outside. The MISSION Act right exists on paper and not in the scheduler’s screen.
Outside records never make it back. OIG found that of nearly 3 million closed community-care consults in one review window, a large share were closed without the outside notes in the VA chart, and tens of thousands sat open more than 90 days past the appointment. The veteran was treated. The VA file says he was not, or says nothing. The next clinician treats the gap as no history.
The claim exam is built to deny. VA must order a C&P exam when the file shows a current disability, an in-service event, and any indication of a link. It often does not. When it does, examiners check “less likely than not” with no rationale, ignore lay statements, and do not review the file. Under Barr v. Nicholson that exam is legally inadequate. VA denies on it anyway. The appeal finds the duty-to-assist error years later and sends it back for another exam by the same system.
A missed C&P is treated as abandonment. Miss the exam without what VA calls good cause and the claim can be denied for failure to report. The veteran’s own medical records do not fill the hole. Rescheduling is a favor, not a right, once they have marked him absent.
Private evidence is discounted on sight. A treating doctor’s nexus or DBQ is called less probative than a VA examiner who saw him once. The file then says the favorable opinion was “not adequate,” and the denial rests on the VA opinion alone.

AN ELECTION COMMISSION MUST BE INDEPENDENT — AND MUST ALSO BE SEEN TO BE INDEPENDENT

The appointment of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar has renewed a fundamental democratic question:

Who gets to choose the people who oversee our elections?

The 2023 law changed the selection committee created by the Supreme Court's Anoop Baranwal judgment.

The Court's interim arrangement had included:

Prime Minister + Leader of Opposition + Chief Justice of India.

Parliament's 2023 law replaced the CJI with a Union Cabinet Minister nominated by the Prime Minister.

That means the three-member committee now consists of the Prime Minister, the Leader of Opposition and a Union Cabinet Minister—giving the government two members on the panel.

Gyanesh Kumar was subsequently appointed CEC in February 2025 under this new framework.

The issue is not whether one individual should be presumed guilty of bias.

The deeper institutional question is:

Does the appointment mechanism provide sufficient independence from the executive—and does it inspire public confidence in electoral neutrality?

That question is now before the Supreme Court. In September 2026, a two-judge bench referred challenges to the 2023 appointment law to the Chief Justice for consideration of a Constitution Bench.

Elections are not merely about voting.

They depend upon public confidence in the institution that prepares the rolls, conducts the process and declares the results.

An Election Commission must not merely be independent.
Its independence must be credible, visible and institutionally protected.

Democracy cannot afford an election referee whose method of appointment itself remains a subject of constitutional dispute.

THE QUESTION IS NO LONGER JUST POLITICAL. IT IS INSTITUTIONAL.

India's Election Commission is now facing scrutiny not merely from opposition politicians or activists, but from questions reportedly raised inside the Commission itself.

The Indian Express investigation reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi placed objections on record at least 14 times over ten months, concerning matters including voter registration, deletion and restoration of names, and electoral-roll technology. 

The story did not remain confined to India.

Al Jazeera, Deutsche Welle and other international media have examined the controversy, including the reported internal disagreements and the questions surrounding SIR and ECINET. 

But there is an equally important fact: the ECI disputes the interpretation of these internal notes, saying differing views are a normal part of institutional deliberation and that its final decisions were lawful and unanimous. 

That is precisely why the issue deserves evidence, transparency and independent scrutiny—not slogans alone.

If voter rolls can determine who participates in democracy, then citizens have a legitimate interest in knowing:

Who authorised each deletion?
Who could alter the database?
What audit trail exists?
Why were objections recorded?
How were wrongly affected voters restored?
And who bears responsibility when the system fails?

Democratic resistance need not mean accepting every allegation as proven. It means refusing to treat serious institutional questions as something that citizens should simply ignore.

The ballot is the citizen's voice.
The electoral roll determines whose voice enters the ballot box.
That makes transparency in the electoral roll a democratic necessity—not a partisan luxury.

text:
*Elon Musk’s Starlink was trying to beat Jio in India*

*But Jio used its 1st mover’s advantage to stop them in their tracks*

*The SHOCKER? Indian Gov is changing a 138 year old law that will bring Starlink back in the game*

*Here’s how Elon is rethinking internet & can possibly kill Jio:*

In 2016, when most of us were witnessing a business disruption standing in queues to get our hands on the free Jio sim card,

12,869 miles away at Rocket Road, California, a group of engineers were planning a technological disruption.

Their goal? Rethink internet access.

Their solution? Satellite Internet.

Traditionally, we have been using internet that relies on cable wires, fiber optic lines, or cellular networks.

But making cable wires or fiber optic lines available in remote villages and hard terrains is not only costly but highly impractical as well.

And this is where satellite internet and Starlink by Elon Musk comes in.

Satellite Internet uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth.

And Starlink is a collection of thousands of small satellites orbiting around 350 miles above the Earth.

For the satellite internet to work, the user on the ground connects to the Starlink dish, known as the user terminal.

The user terminal communicates with nearby Starlink satellites and forms a link to the larger Starlink network

The satellites then form a mesh network, that allows them to pass data between each other and create global network coverage.

Starlink’s motto is — ‘virtually anywhere on earth without wires or cellphone towers.’

It started its operation in 2019 and true to its motto, it’s already available in over 65 countries,

— covering all 7 continents (including Antarctica!)

But Starlink hasn’t been able to make any progress in India.

Last year, it registered its business in India via a local unit Starlink Satellite Communications Pvt Ltd.

The company had planned to provide fast internet data in the Indian market at a subsidized price compared to the international market.

It had received 5,000+ pre-orders.

But the government said Starlink Internet Services doesn’t have the license to offer services in India.

And it asked Starlink to return people’s money.

Now, one company’s loss is another company’s gain.

In Feb this year, Reliance Jio partnered up with Luxembourg-based SES to provide satellite-based broadband services in India.

And created a joint venture called — Jio Space Technology Ltd.

Moreover, Starlink and Jio Space aren’t the only contenders for India’s space spectrum.

OneWeb is backed by Airtel in India and Hughes Communication.

Tata group entity Nelco partnered up with Canada's Telesat.

And Amazon’s Kuiper is going to launch satellites in 2024.

But why are so many companies vying for India’s space spectrum?

India has a population of 1.4 billion out of which 40% do not have internet access because they are in rural and remote areas.

And traditional terrestrial networks are not easy to install.

Hence, India’s satellite broadband service is expected to reach $1.9 billion by 2030, growing at a CAGR of 36%.

Now, because India has so many contenders for its spectrum, the question arises — who should get it?

Starlink and OneWeb wanted the government to assign licenses to companies, since spectrum is a natural resource that should be shared by companies.

But Jio wanted the government to auction the spectrum like it did with 4G & 5G 👀

Finally, the government brought in some reforms and firstly dedicated a sole agency IN-SPACe to authorize space activities for both government and private satellite communication companies.

And a bill has been proposed to replace the 138-year-old Indian Telegraph Act that currently governs the telecommunication sector.

So now, both Jio Space & OneWeb have received their GMPCS license from the Department of Telecommunications in India.

And Starlink is 3rd in line to receive the GMPCS license.

I’ve put the complaint, the exhibits and the older company records together because I want people to be able to follow this case without having to piece it together from screenshots and replies.

That includes both sides. Korra says he received court documents, denies the allegations and says none of this happened. His denial needs to be included.

X filed its lawsuit against Immortal Snail LLC on September 28, 2026, in the Northern District of Texas. The case number is 4:26-cv-01254. Immortal Snail is the only named defendant in the federal case. Being mentioned in the complaint doesn’t automatically make someone else a defendant.

This is a civil lawsuit about contracts, suspended accounts and arbitration. X wants to stop the arbitration brought by Snail and is suing for breach of contract. There’s no judgment in the material I’ve reviewed establishing the bribery, unauthorized-access or impersonation allegations as proven. The complaint doesn’t bring a standalone RICO claim either, although RICO comes up in an earlier letter.

The complaint itself is 31 pages. The ECF 1 package I reviewed runs to 288 pages, including the cover sheet, index and 25 exhibits. Those exhibits matter because they also include Snail’s account, letters from its lawyers, contracts and commercial records. This package isn’t the entire, up-to-date court file.

One document deserves particular attention: the January 12, 2026 letter from their own lawyers.

Kevin C. Kaplan and Christopher E. Cheek, of Coffey Burlington, say they represent Immortal Snail, Moonrail Limited B.V. and Ossi Ketola. They describe Ketola as the “principal and owner” of both companies. The letter is part of Snail’s arbitration claim, included in Exhibit 25, pages 17–18.

If you have a claim or ongoing proceedings against Ketola involving Duel or CSGOEmpire, that’s a document worth putting in front of your lawyer. It gives them a specific statement from his stated representatives to consider when looking at ownership, corporate relationships and who belongs in your case. The separate companies, directors and representatives have to be considered alongside that statement.

The letter doesn’t settle personal liability, give ownership percentages or establish that one company is a subsidiary of the other. It also doesn’t prove that the companies are fictitious or their directors are acting as fronts. What it does record is how those lawyers described their clients and Ketola’s ownership.

The platforms’ own terms identify the companies:

Duel: Immortal Snail LLC, Nevis, registration L22982.
CSGOEmpire: Moonrail Limited B.V., Curaçao, registration 148182.
Payments for Moonrail may be handled by JHOLT LTD, Cyprus, registration HE393291, under an agreement between the two companies.

Moonrail also appears in DUEL’s trademark records. The official Israeli register lists it as the owner of trademark 374583, registered on May 5, 2025. In Canada, Moonrail filed DUEL application 2342187 on August 6, 2024. The Canadian record names David S. Lipkus of Lipkus Law LLP as the trademark agent and records the application as abandoned under section 36 on July 17, 2026.

That abandonment concerns the Canadian application. It doesn’t mean every DUEL trademark was cancelled or the platform stopped operating. And these records describe different jobs: owning a trademark, operating a platform, processing payments and representing a trademark applicant aren’t interchangeable roles.

The account history in X’s complaint starts in 2024, before the purchases people are discussing.

X alleges that on March 25, 2024, Ketola and Snail took control of an account using @duel, changed its email to a Moonrail mailbox and used it to promote a casino. X says it suspended the account on March 27, after which attempts to recover it involved intermediaries and access to employees. [Paragraphs 36–39.]

X also alleges that Ketola and CSGOEmpire were involved in an intrusion into @CSGORoll reported in April 2024. It cites a livestream in which, according to the complaint, Ketola celebrated what happened, mentioned “Sticky Hand” and said he worked for him. I haven’t authenticated the original video. X says it suspended @JNSAST the following day after reports of targeted harassment, disclosure of personal information and threats. [Paragraphs 28–29.]

The complaint goes on to describe what X calls bribery and unauthorized account reinstatements. It alleges that internal information about @duel was obtained in June 2024 and usernames were changed to move @monarch to another account. It also says an employee photographed internal information in July after a $1,500 offer and was fired. Further reinstatements through contractors and further suspensions followed, according to X. [Paragraphs 39, 40 and 44–49.]

There’s a company letter in this part of the file too. Exhibit 3 contains Moonrail’s July 9, 2024 authorization for Dušan Pećić to represent it. The names beneath the signatures are Lorenza Godett and Christopher van Rosberg, acting for Xecutive Corporate Management B.V., which is identified as a director of Moonrail. HLTV also named Pećić as CSGOEmpire’s marketing manager in March 2024.

The letter authorizes representation. It doesn’t authorize hacking, bribery or threats, or show that its signatories knew about the conduct X alleges.

The dates also need to stay as written. X dates Pećić’s appeal to June 28, 2024, but the authorization letter is dated July 9. Paragraph 47 then dates the rejection to July 13, 2025. I’m not going to quietly change those dates to make them line up.

Haci Isik appears as an intermediary. X says he was engaged in December 2024 to recover @duel and looked for insiders willing to reactivate or suspend accounts for money. It says he later tried to buy the handle directly, presenting an esports and FPS gaming project in February 2025. That’s X’s description of the discussions and their purpose. [Paragraphs 41–43.]

Paragraph 43 names two different payers: according to X, Moonrail paid for @duel_temp’s Premium subscription, while Immortal Snail paid for @duel itself. The person negotiating, the subscription payer and the handle buyer have different roles in that account. We don’t have the full negotiation or complete banking records in this package.

The acquisition documents total $480,000:

A $300,000 invoice for @Duel, dated March 24, 2025.
An $80,000 invoice for @Monarch, dated April 16.
A $100,000 receipt for @Castle, paid on June 3.

Snail says it paid all three. But two documents are invoices and one is a receipt, so I’m not calling them three bank payment confirmations. The @Castle receipt says “Crypto.” It gives no wallet, network, asset or transaction hash to trace. [Exhibit 25, pp. 13–15.]

A handle can move between accounts. The 2024 events and the 2025 purchases don’t establish that one person continuously owned one underlying account.

Then there’s the Grizzly section shown in the screenshot.

X describes Grizzly as a former CSGOEmpire Product Manager who fell out with Ketola. It alleges that Ketola and Snail accessed one of his accounts without authorization in February 2025, after he published internal conversations. [Paragraph 30.]

According to X, the Discord and Telegram conversations discussed accessing Israeli government email accounts and using them to ask platforms to remove competitors’ accounts, including CSGORoll. The complaint also describes discussions about wording those requests to make them look like legitimate official requests.

The original emails and their headers aren’t in the package I reviewed, and I haven’t independently verified who controlled those mailboxes. None of this establishes involvement by the Israeli government.

Paragraph 31 quotes Grizzly claiming to have more than 6.5 GB of chat exports and other evidence. In that quoted post, he said the material included plans to disclose relatives’ personal information and references to physical attacks against Stake. He also said he feared for his life and was looking for a journalist to receive the files.

The full archive isn’t here. His statement that he had it doesn’t tell us whether he delivered it to X, a journalist or an authority.

Paragraph 32 describes a video conversation between “Gr1zzly” and “Monarch,” whom X identifies as Ketola. X attributes to Monarch references to Bosnian mafia contacts, plans for kidnappings and possible murders, obtaining personal information, services involving violence and statements about mutilations.

Those are exceptionally serious allegations. I haven’t authenticated the original video, and I don’t have independent evidence establishing that the acts described were carried out. I’m reporting what X attributes to that conversation.

Paragraph 33 describes another conversation, on Telegram, about using government emails to get accounts removed, with language involving escalation and violence. Here the complaint calls the participant “Ossi” and says he is presumably Ossi Ketola. “Presumably” is in the document. It stays in this account too.

X says one of Grizzly’s accounts was taken over, had its biography changed from “Ex-CSGOEmpire” to a message saying it had been seized by @theJNSAST, then was used to promote Duel. It also cites @monarchlawyer announcing an account takeover. A username containing “lawyer” doesn’t establish that the person using it is one. [Paragraph 34.]

Korra expressly denies these events in the post being quoted. That denial belongs alongside the allegations. I also couldn’t retrieve the original links in footnotes 15–18 in readable form, so the complaint and screenshots aren’t a substitute for authenticating the underlying material.

X makes a technical claim as well. Footnote 15 says @fastschitzobear, @CSGOEmpire, @CSGOEmpireV2, @duel and @monarch used the same Known Device Token. X treats that as evidence of previous access through the same device or browser and an indication of collaboration. Paragraph 50 also refers to matches involving devices, software, identifiers, cookies and financial accounts.

The complete logs and dates needed to check that conclusion aren’t in the package. A shared device doesn’t tell us who wrote a particular message, or whether the overlap happened before or after an account takeover.

There are further allegations about accounts critical of the business.

Paragraph 35 describes a trademark complaint with allegedly manipulated documents against a former CSGOEmpire social media manager. That role shouldn’t automatically be treated as the Product Manager role attributed to Grizzly. In paragraph 52, X alleges that Isik offered in June 2025 to find insiders who would suspend accounts critical of Ketola and his companies. These remain allegations in the material reviewed.

X says it suspended @duel, @monarch and @castle, along with related accounts, around October 21, 2025. It alleges that requests impersonating a US law firm followed, as did a $300,000 offer to an employee to reactivate accounts. Exhibits 1 and 2 contain the November letters X disputes. Paragraph 56 doesn’t give the exact date of the alleged offer.

There are two different $300,000 figures here. The first is the invoiced purchase price for @Duel. The second is an alleged bribe in a later incident. They shouldn’t be merged.

Paragraph 58 describes a May 2026 request that X says impersonated the Malaysian police, followed by complaints in India. The exhibits show the request fields, but they don’t authenticate the senders. I’m leaving out the names of people who may themselves have been impersonated.

X mentions Arya A. when linking an email identifier used in requests with one in billing documents. That is X’s attribution. It doesn’t establish a company position or authorship of every communication.

Snail’s side is in the file too, and it deserves to be read.

Its arbitration claim says it paid for the handles and then lost access without an adequate explanation, harming its business, reputation and commercial expectations. It wants the accounts restored and compensation. It also raises possible interference by competitors or an X shareholder connected to competitors. The material I reviewed neither names that shareholder nor establishes that theory. [Exhibit 25, pp. 4–8.]

Snail started arbitration in April 2026. X says the relevant contracts require disputes to go to Texas courts. Mohamed F. Sweify was appointed arbitrator in July. Kaplan and Cheek attended an August preliminary hearing; X had said it wouldn’t participate and maintained that position. The arbitration order put jurisdiction first.

Part of the dispute is which terms apply. The 2024 handle-transfer terms select a Texas forum, reserve suspension rights and include a $100 limit on liability. Snail relies on the October 2025 Marketplace terms, which include arbitration subject to US residency. How those terms apply here is a question in the case, not something this post resolves.

X’s September letter mentioned possible legal actions, including RICO. That doesn’t turn this into a filed RICO claim, a criminal prosecution or an established FBI investigation.

The federal complaint names Caitlin A. Halpern and Lauryn E. Bennett of Gibbs & Bruns, and Charles W. Fillmore of Brown Pruitt, as X’s lawyers. The public docket records the case’s reassignment to Reed O’Connor on September 30. A lawyer’s representation of a party doesn’t make them responsible for the conduct being disputed.

The older company records help explain the business relationships. They need to be read with their own limits: these are supplied historical copies, and I haven’t independently certified every file’s authenticity or confirmed its official receipt. The X lawsuit doesn’t authenticate the rest of the archive.

An August 2023 organizational chart shows Ossi owning 100% of Moonrail and Moonrail owning 100% of JHOLT. That tells us what the chart records at that time; it isn’t a current ownership certificate. [D026.]

Moonrail’s shareholders’ register goes further back. The copy marked D027 reproduces a certification dated July 29, 2024. It records Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. subscribing for all 10,000 shares on October 1, 2018, then transferring them the next day. That initial shareholding is a separate role from its later corporate administration work.

The register lists these corporate holdings from October 2, 2018, and their later transfers:

JPellikka Oy, Finland, 2881789-9: 13.65%, later recorded under Day Star Enterprises OÜ, Estonia, 14630609.
Hiirijoki & Partners Oy, Finland, 2887371-9: 12.50%, later recorded under Rotten Apples OÜ, Estonia, 14631261.
create.repeat Oy, Finland, 2662670-6: 13.65%, later recorded under Simple Holdings OÜ, Estonia, 14635334.

It dates those three transfers to December 17, 2018. It then records Ketola, who already held 44.80%, acquiring the remaining 55.20% on November 13, 2019. That remaining stake consists of the three company holdings totaling 39.80%, plus an individual holding of 15.40%.

Those entries don’t tell us the purchase price or show the payments. They also don’t make those companies current owners of Duel. [D027, pp. 3–4.]

The Estonian public register confirms the companies’ identities and gives these dates:

Day Star: registered December 21, 2018; deleted from the register August 13, 2021.
Rotten Apples: registered December 27, 2018; deleted September 8, 2021.
Simple Holdings: registered January 4, 2019; deleted November 26, 2021.

All three registration dates are later than the December 17 transfer date in Moonrail’s book. That needs an explanation from the underlying documents. I can’t resolve the legally effective transfer dates from these records or call the discrepancy proof of forgery. The public company records establish those companies’ existence; the link to Moonrail’s shares comes from the supplied shareholders’ register.

Finland’s register also shows that JPellikka Oy became Veivi Ventures Oy on January 18, 2023. A later name change doesn’t establish a present-day stake in Moonrail.

There’s more on the earlier funding in a November 14, 2025 letter addressed to the Curaçao Gaming Authority. Moonrail says its initial funding came from Ketola’s earlier business activities through Global Vault oy and the distribution of that company’s assets after liquidation.

Global Vault’s Finnish registration number is 2793380-4. It was registered on November 9, 2016, and dissolved on April 1, 2019. The register confirms those facts. The explanation connecting its funds to Moonrail comes from Moonrail’s letter; it isn’t bank verification and doesn’t establish that Global Vault operated CSGOEmpire. [D050, pp. 1–3.]

The historical PRH/Virre extract issued on August 14, 2026 lists Ossi Eemeli Ketola as Global Vault’s board member and managing director from November 9, 2016 to July 5, 2018. It lists Satu Maarit Ketola as a deputy board member over the same period, and Lari Hiirijoki as a procurist, meaning a holder of a commercial power of attorney, from November 2017. His later appointment as liquidator was registered on July 5, 2018.

Those are documented business roles. They don’t establish family relationships or positions for those other individuals at today’s operators. [Global Vault PRH/Virre extract, pp. 1–3.]

The January 18, 2019 liquidator’s report in D050 identifies Ketola as holding all 100 shares and the rights to Global Vault’s asset distribution. Lari Hiirijoki signs as liquidator. This adds to the ownership and funding history, but it still doesn’t supply the records of transfers between the people and companies involved. [D050, pp. 10–11.]

There’s a one-year difference between two documents that I’m keeping visible. Moonrail’s November 2025 letter says Ketola owned 100% of Moonrail from November 13, 2018. The shareholders’ register puts his purchase of the final 55.20% on November 13, 2019. I don’t have enough to settle which date is correct.

The same letter gives Moonrail’s licensing account: Cyberluck N.V. in 2018, Antillephone N.V. in 2021, then the Gaming Control Board/Curaçao Gaming Authority framework. That is Moonrail’s account of its sublicensing and licensing history. It doesn’t establish permission to operate everywhere, and it can’t simply be applied to Immortal Snail. [D050, p. 1.]

The February 2025 assessment in the archive identifies missing documentation and recommends conditions covering management identification, anti-money-laundering measures, responsible gambling, territorial access and media policy. These are recommendations, not a sanction or proof that every proposed condition was imposed. [D029.]

A later business plan, identified in the archive as October 30, 2025, names Irene Rosenblatt as CEO, Matt Tanner as CFO and Sampsa Saarela as CTO. It names Rokas Daugirdas as compliance manager and Pearl Reiph as MLRO, the money-laundering reporting role. Xecutive is described as the board, with the CEO responsible for daily operations and reporting to it. Those are the roles this historical plan gives them. I haven’t verified that they still hold them, and the titles don’t prove involvement in X’s allegations. [D041, pp. 1–2 and 4–5.]

Moonrail’s advertising policy is worth reading in full as well. Version 1.0, dated May 29, 2025, requires prior advertising review, influencer agreements, sponsorship disclosure and territorial controls. It prohibits presenting gambling as a solution to financial difficulties, associating it with violence or dangerous behavior, and using content or influencers that appeal to minors. Advertising materials require compliance approval. Moonrail and its agents are also prohibited from offering players credit or loans to gamble. [D037, pp. 4–6.]

Those are written rules for Moonrail at that date. To assess a particular campaign against them, we’d still need to check the campaign itself, when it ran and which policy applied. Having a policy doesn’t tell us how it was followed in every case.

The archive also contains an August 1, 2025 response attributed to Xecutive on Moonrail’s behalf about Coffeezilla. It denies bribery. It says former managers proposed investigating a competitor without senior authorization, denies asking anyone to suppress or change coverage of Moonrail, and says the people who acted without authorization were removed. They aren’t named. The letter describes the owner as providing strategic guidance, separate from operational campaigns. That response needs to accompany the allegation. [D038.]

The August and November 2025 letters both present Xecutive Corporate Management B.V. as a director of Moonrail. Their signature blocks name Analissa Heiland and Lorenza Godett as its representatives. That establishes how they are presented in those letters, not participation in the alleged conduct. These letters and the other historical copies remain subject to the authenticity and date limitations explained above. [D038, p. 2; D050, p. 2.]

The regulatory decisions have their own official sources.

Spain’s decision ES/2025/011 imposes a €5 million fine and a four-year disqualification from conducting gambling activities on Moonrail for operating without the required Spanish authorization. It identifies CSGOEmpire and orders the activity to stop. The DGOJ announced the sanction in November 2025. I haven’t verified whether it was paid or the outcome of any appeals.

Sweden prohibited Moonrail from providing gambling without the required license in a decision dated November 2, 2023. Denmark’s official list includes https://t.co/wm4kIZPtIu among the domains blocked by court order in July 2023.

Those decisions apply to the countries and dates they cover. They don’t prove X’s allegations of bribery or unauthorized access. A declared Curaçao or Anjouan license doesn’t establish permission to operate in every other market either.

For people with disputes over balances or affiliate earnings, the terms themselves also matter. CSGOEmpire’s terms, marked as updated on July 7, 2026, promise withdrawals even when an account is closed and, where necessary, compensation for unclaimed referral earnings or rewards. They also contain exceptions and restrictions for abuse, self-referrals, dormant accounts and reversed trades. Any particular withholding needs to be checked against the terms that applied, the clause relied on and the account records. The page alone doesn’t prove a breach in someone’s case.

I also need to be open about my own position. I’ve filed a police complaint over a separate dispute. It records my allegations; it isn’t a judgment proving them. X’s case doesn’t settle my claims either. I’m leaving out amounts that still need reconciliation and keeping the two proceedings separate.

What we have here is a civil complaint, Snail’s arbitration claim, commercial records, a letter from lawyers describing Ketola’s ownership of both operators, historical company documents and official regulatory decisions. The most serious allegations in the complaint haven’t been established as proven in the material I’ve reviewed.

If I’ve got a document, page or date wrong, point me to it. I’ll correct it. I’ll also include responses supported by documents.

Read the comments under my post below if you want to see how quickly surveillance and control is becoming normalised. People are persuaded that removing their own privacy is necessary for safety.

Apple removed Bitchat from its Indian App Store after a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology under Section 69A. Apple’s notice said “the app contained content that was illegal” in India, but Bitchat is decentralised messaging software. The app can’t contain illegal content any more than its own Messages app.

This wasn’t the first attempt to restrict it. In July, Indian authorities targeted Bitchat’s open source repositories because the software can operate without internet access, continue working when the government shuts down the Internet. 

Indian digital rights lawyers question the legal basis for targeting an app because of what its architecture allows rather than because of specific illegal material. 

A lot of the replies to me amount to the same argument: terrorism, crime or national security means the government should be allowed to remove private communication tools.

That argument should frighten people far more than Apple’s censorship.

India isn’t unique. The same political conditioning is happening in the US, UK, Australia and across Europe. Governments are telling people that less privacy, more identity verification, more interception and more monitoring are necessary for safety.

People are being encouraged to believe that surveillance protects them and private communications protect criminals.

Once a society accepts that premise, every privacy technology becomes suspicious by design. Encryption becomes obstruction. Anonymous communication becomes evasion. Offline messaging becomes a way to bypass government controls. Refusing to identify yourself becomes something that needs explaining.

That’s how private communication stops being treated as a normal civil liberty and starts being treated as a privilege government can withdraw.

Some of the replies have also become personal and racial because people appear to have decided what I must think about India based on what they assume about me.

So let me make that part clear.

I’ve spent years working directly with communities in India. My daughter is half Indian. I’ve travelled there many times. The charity I co-founded 14 years ago held FCRA status and worked at grassroots level because we wanted money and decisions to stay with the communities we were helping.

We helped people open bank accounts, taught financial literacy, worked with families affected by domestic violence, and helped women and girls gain access to their own sanitation.

Each village and slum decided who needed help most. Our CEO was local and had spent 20 years working in related fields, which meant communities trusted him. Community federations shared in the low-interest repayments so they could continue operating locally.

When loans were repaid, the money funded more loans. No money was taken out of India. Even though we no longer operate there, that money continues to be recycled so more toilets can be built and more small businesses can be funded. When somebody couldn’t repay, which was rare, we supported them instead of treating them like a failed account.

Our CEO also regularly had police turn up looking for bribes. We eventually stopped because operating legitimately became extraordinarily difficult.

I can care deeply about India and still criticise its government.

Caring about the people of a country is why I care when their government removes technology that allows them to communicate privately, especially when it’s  designed to keep working when the government shut down the internet to extinguish freedom of speech and civil liberties.

Criticising surveillance isn’t criticism of Indians.

And Indians deserve privacy and civil liberties every bit as much as people in the US, UK, Australia or Europe.

In Constituent Assembly, Mr Tajamul Hussain argued that Muslims should not be given reservation but scheduled caste should be given. The excerpts are enclosed below 

Mr. President, Sir, reservation of seats in any shape or form and for any community or group of people is, in my opinion, absolutely wrong in principle. Therefore I am strongly of opinion that there should be no reservation of seats for anyone and I, as a Muslim, speak for the Muslims. There should be no reservation of seats for the Muslim community. (Hear, Hear). I would like to tell you that in no civilised country where there is parliamentary system on democratic lines, there is any reservation of seats. Take the case of England. The House of Commons is the mother of parliaments. There is no reservation of seats for community there. No doubt they had reservation of seats for the universities but even that has been abolished. What is reservation, Sir? Reservation is nothing but a concession, a safeguard a protection for the weak. We, Muslims do not want any concession. Do not want protection, do not want safeguards. We are not weak. This concession would do more harm than good to the Muslims. Reservation is forcing candidates on unwilling electorates. Whether the electorates wants us or not, we thrust ourselves on them. We do not want to thrust ourselves on unwilling electorates. The majority community will naturally think that we are encroaching upon their rights. We do not want them to think that. We must expert ourselves. Separate electorates have been a curse to India, have done incalculable harm to this country. It was invented by the British. Reservation is the offspring of separate electorates. Do not bring in reservation in the place of separate electorates. Separate electorates have barred our progress. Separate electorates have gone for ever. We desire neither reservation nor separate electorates. We want to merge in the nation. We desire to stand on our own legs. We do not want the support of anyone. We are not weak. We are strong. We are Indians first and we are all Indians and will remain Indians. We shall fight for the honour and glory of India and we shall die for it. (Applause). We shall stand united. There will be no divisions amongst Indians. United we stand; divided we fall. Therefore we do not want reservation. It means division. I ask the members of the majority community who are present here today:-Will you allow us to stand on our legs? Will you allow us to be a part and parcel of the nation? Will you us to be an  equal partner with you? Will you allow us to march shoulder to shoulder with you? Will you allow us to share your sorrows grief and joy? If you do, then for god’s sake keep your hands off reservation for the Muslim community. We do not want statutory safeguard. As I said before, we must stand on our own legs. If we do that, we will have no inferiority complex. We are not inferior to you in any way, Do not make us feel inferior by giving us this concession. I say emphatically there is no difference between you and me. Because we worship the same God by different names, in a different way, that is no reason why we should be considered a minority. We are not a minority. The term ‘minority’ is a British creation. The British created minorities. The British have gone and minorities have gone with them. Remove the term ‘minority’ from your dictionary. (Hear, Hear). There is no minority in India. Only so long as there were separate electorates and reservation of seats there was a majority community and a minority community.

I ask the majority community not to distrust the minorities now. The minorities have adjusted themselves. I will give you a concrete example. You remember the Hyderabad incident; you remember that before you took police action against Hyderabad, what happened. The majority community were afraid that there would be rioting of the Muslims if action was taken against Hyderabad. I was first man to speak about it about a year and half ago in the Central Legislature. I criticised the Government of India. I am sorry Sardar Patel was not present at that time when I was dealing with his portfolio, but my honourable Friend Mr. Gadgil was in charge. I criticised the action of the Government, I told them that they were absolutely mistaken in thinking that the Muslims would rise; they would adjust themselves. I said to them: “You march an army against Hyderabad and within couple of days, you would take the whole of Hyderabad.” I made a long speech and after my speech was over, there was a reply by the Honourable Minister in charge, Mr. Gadgil. He never spoke a single word about it and he never replied to my criticism, but I asked him: “You have replied to everybody’s criticism. Why not mine? I asked you to march an army against Hyderabad; you would take Hyderabad within a couple of days and there would be no rioting.” Mr. Gadgil “You are perfectly right and we will do it.”

I appeal to all minorities to join the majority in creating a secular State. In the new state of things, I want that every citizen in India should be able to rise to the fullest stature and that is why I say that reservation would be suicidal to the minority. I want the minorities to forget that they are minorities in politics. If they think they are minorities in politics, they will be isolated. If they are isolated, the feeling of frustration will cripple them. I do not want to remain minority. Do the minorities, I ask, expect to form part of the great nation and have a hand in the control of its destinies. Can they achieve that aspiration if they are isolated from the rest of India? The minorities if they are returned as minorities, i.e., by reservation of seats can never have an effective voice in the affairs of the country. They can never form a Government. Disraeli could never have formed a Government and could never have become the Prime Minister of England had there been reservation of seats for the Jews in England. I want the minorities to have an honourable place in the Union of India. National interests must always be placed over group interests. The minorities should look forward to the time when they could take their place not under communal or racial labels, but as part and parcel of the whole Indian community.

Now, Sir, with your permission, I want to say a few words with regard to the speeches made against the motion of Sardar Patel. I take first Mr. Muhammad Ismail of Madras. He wants separate electorate. I appeal to his not to ask the charity. Asking for separate electorates is nothing but asking for charity. I tell him that the consequences will be terrible. The majority community will never trust you then. You will never be able to expert yourself. You will be isolated, you will be treated as an alien and your position will be the same as that of the Scheduled Caste. You are not poor. Like the Scheduled Castes, you are not weak, you are not uneducated; you are not uncultured; you can always support yourself. You have produced brilliant men. So do not ask for protection or safeguard. You must have self-confidence in you.  You must expert yourself. You must get into the Assembly by open competition. The times have changed. Adjust yourself. You admitted yesterday in your speech that the atmosphere is better now. I entirely agree with you that the atmosphere is better now. I appeal to you, do not spoil that atmosphere. Improve it, but do not spoil it and if you insist on separate electorate, you will spoil atmosphere very badly. If you get separate electorates, it will again become as bad as before. Say to yourself, Mr. Ismail, that you are an Indian first and an Indian last. Then you will forget all about separate electorates. You will never think of it again.

I will tell you, Sir, that when I had sent in my amendment to clause 292 that it should be deleted, that there should be no reservation of seats, then several Muslim friends to mine, who were for reservation of seats asked me. “Do you realize that the mentality of the Hindus is such at present that if there were no reservation of seats for the Muslims, the Muslims can never succeed?” That honourable gentleman for whom I have got great esteem told me: “Look at us. We have always been with the Congress; we have been to jail and all that. No doubt we will get a ticket from the Congress; many Muslims will get tickets from Socialists and Communists and from other organisations, but what about the electorates? They will never elect you and they will never elect us. So, if there is no reservation, no Muslims will get in because of the mentality of the Hindus.” I told him, Sir, what I am telling you now. I said that I entirely agreed with him that the mentality of the Hindus is such at present. I say to Mr. Ismail also that as long as there is reservation of seats or separate electorate the mentality of the Hindus will never change. You do away with these two things and the mentality will automatically change. I do not want to go into the history of this mentality. I am not going to apportion blame as that will take a long time and you have allotted me a short time and I want to be brief and finish my speech within that time. You all know how the mentality of the Hindus became such, but we have to live in this country, we must change their mentality and it is our duty to change their mentality and the only way the mentality can be changed is to become a part and parcel of the Indian Union. You should say that they are no longer our enemies and then they will be like brothers to us.

Now, Sir, with regard to Mr. Lari, he does not want separate electorates; he does not want reservation of seats; he has condemned both the systems and he says that both the systems are dangerous. He has said that, and I entirely agree with him. He has always opposed separate electorates, reservation of seats and the partition of the country. He is right. But he wants cumulative voting, that is, proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote, or something like that. My honourable Friend, Mr. Saksena has told us that it is a very cumbrous system of mathematical calculations; I am not dealing with that now. The only thing I want to say is that Mr. Lari wants to get into the Assembly by the back door. For example suppose there is a constituency that has to elect four candidates for the House or the People, and there are five candidates. One will be defeated and four will be elected. Out of these five, four are Hindus and one is a Muslim. The votes of the Hindus will be divided among the Hindus and there will get elected. The Muslim will get in on the Muslim votes. Again separate electorates, again reservation of seats. I should like to say to my honourable Friend Mr. Lari if I may say so, that is worse than separate electorate, as the method is not clean. It is not straightforward. I quite understand Mr. Mohamed Ismail’s view when he asks for separate electorates. That is a straightforward method. What is this back-door method of Mr. Lari. I do not understand. I am sure the Muslims do not like these crooked methods; they want a straight, honourable fight. In spite of the fact that Mr. Lari has always openly opposed Pakistan, separate electorates and reservation of seats he still feels inferiority complex. I would ask him to shed this inferiority complex. The country will change for the better.

Last of all, I come to the speech of my honourable and esteemed friend, for whom I have very great regard, Sir Saadulla, the Ex-Premier of Assam. He complains before us that the majority of the Muslim members of the Advisory Committee on Minorities Fundamental Rights etc., did not support the resolution that there should be no reservation of seats for the Muslims. I have already told you, Sir, that I have very great esteem and regard for the Ex-premier of Assam, but I am afraid I must differ from him on this point. I sent my resolution to the Committee to the effect that there should be no reservation of seats. My resolution was discussed under the Chairmanship of the Honourable Sardar Patel. I spoke on my resolution. Begum Aizaz Rasul supported me. Maulana Azad was present there; he did not oppose me. The only person who opposed me was my honourable friend Jafar Imam, from Bihar. There too, I had a majority: Begum Aizaz Rasul. Maulana Azad and myself as against one. The meeting could not be finished and was adjourned sine die. Then it was held on the 11th of this month. I wanted to attend that meeting, particularly because my resolution was there I wanted to move it again. But I never received notice of the meeting. The notice was lying in Delhi; it never reached me. If I had got notice of the meeting. I would have attended it. When I came to Delhi, I learnt that there was the meeting that day. I was happy to learn that the substance of my resolution had been accepted though I was absent. I sent a statement to the Press why I could not attend the meeting that day and it was published in all the papers. Sir Saadulla could not attend the meeting; I do not know why. That meeting was attended by four honourable members: Maulana Azad, Maulana Hifizur Rahman, Begum Aizaz Rasul and Mr. Jaffar Imam. Maulana Azad and Maulana Hifizur Rehman did not oppose my resolution that there should be no reservation of seats.

Every member of this House does not speak. If he oppose, he opposes. If he does not speak, but says “I vote for it“, then he is with it. Maulana Azad was present. If he wanted to oppose, he would have opposed. The two Maulanas did not oppose begum Aizaz Rasul supported my resolution in substance. The resolution was moved by my honourable Friend Dr. Mookherjee. It was the same as my own. Begum Aizaz Rasul supported it. My honourable Friend Mr. Jaffar Imam opposed it. If the Maulana were not with my resolution, they would have sided with Jafar Imam. They said nothing. Votes were taken. There was a clear majority. The Honourable Sardar Patel, I understand, declared that the Muslims were in favour of the motion in spite of the two Maulanas remaining silent. It means that they were with me: three to one voting: there was a majority.

I believe, -I do not remember exactly-there are seven Muslim members on the Committee. Only two are opposed to my resolution; five are with me. The two who are against me are my Hon’ble friends Sir Saadulla and Mr. Jafar Imam. The five who are in favour are , Maulana Azad, Maulana Hifizur Rahman, Begum Aizaz Rasul, Mr. Husseinboy Laljee and myself. Mr. Laljee’s views are well known. He opposed Mr. Jinnah. I know his views. In fact,he wrote to me once, “For God’s sake do something to remove reservations.” Therefore, I had an overwhelming majority. There was another member Syed Ali Zaheer. He is now an Ambassador; I know his views. He is also of the same view as I am.

The next point of my esteemed Friend Sir Saadulla is this. He says, ‘let us take the vote of the Muslim Members here.’ That is a challenge thrown to us. I accept the challenge. I may remind my honourable Friend Sir Saadulla that when the Muslim members came here to Delhi for the first time there was a meeting of all the Muslim members in Western Court. All of them were present. I was the first man to have got up and said that there should be no reservation of seats. I sent my resolution to the Constituent Assembly when you, Sir, were presiding. I regret to say, except one, not a single member supported me. I found that the Muslims wanted reservation. So, I did not move my resolution. That was the first meeting in which the Muslims were against me. The next meeting was in the house of Nawab Muhammad Ismail, about which he also has told you, in 18, Windsor Place. There my view was accepted by an overwhelming majority. The same Muslim members who were present in the Western Court were present here also, and it was passed by an overwhelming majority that there should be no reservation of seats. See how the time had changed. The only member who opposed it was my honourable Friend Sir Saadulla. He is honestly of that opinion; I respect his view. I hope he will respect my view. He said, ‘no there must be reservation of seats‘. But, one thing he said: ‘personally I am not in favour of reservation, but the Muslims want it’. Most humbly I wish to tell him that he is wrong. The Muslims do not want it. Sir Saadulla was the only opposing member. Then there was the Madras group. They are a group by themselves, Sir, I understand their opinion. They have throughout been saying, ” No reservation, but separate electorates; let us have separate electorates.” At the Western Court, they said, “let us have separate electorate,” at Nawab Ismail Sahib’s place also they asked for separate electorates and here also they ask for separate electorates. They are welcome to their opinion. But that there should be no reservation was passed by an overwhelming majority. All of us were present. And after that I sent in my amendment saying that the whole section be deleted or that there should be no reservation for Muslims.

ICYMI: The Day the Director of Forensic Services in Police Was Ordered by a Judge to Answer Questions as Asked and Not as he Wants Them Asked. 

This was 2 years ago in the still ongoing trial of Uganda Vs MollyKatanga and 4 others. 

Mr Andrew K. Mubiru had just finished giving DNA forensic evidence on behalf of the state.

He had told court that he had analyzed and reported DNA evidence in the trial.

Time for cross examination came and the defense put it on the record that the state had denied them most of the documents pertaining to the tests Mr Mubiru had conducted; same tests the state wanted to rely on to secure convictions against their clients.

The state on their part said they weren’t under duty to disclose laboratory protocols, procedures or any such background information. But they had disclosed the final DNA report. The methods used to get it be damned or they were a national security issue.

But they offered their witness to be cross examined on that.

Defense Attorney @elisonk took the first stab at it.

Judge Isaac Muwata to Mr Elison Karuhanga: You can proceed with cross examination 
EK: Much obliged my Lord. For the record, Elison Karuhanga….

Mr Mubiru, you prepared a report for purposes of this hearing, correct? Yes?
AM: That’s true, my Lord
EK: You’ll agree with me that this report contains all the tests you carried out on the exhibits in this case?
AM: My Lord all the tests that we conduct, the outcomes and findings, we detail them in a report that is submitted to court.
Judge: No, you refer to this report, not to others
AM: This report, my Lord 
EK: My Lord, let me ask the question again. 
Mr Mubiru, you’ll agree that this report contains all the tests you carried out on the exhibits that you received. 
AM: My Lord the tests conducted on the exhibits I received are detailed in the report that is submitted to court.
EK: You’ll also agree that the report contains all the exhibits you received in this case?
AM: My Lord, the exhibits I received are detailed in the report that is submitted to court
EK: I think if you just help us quicken the answers with yes or no where yes or no can do…
AM: My Lord the exhibits that I received and examined are detailed in the report that is submitted to court
EK: So, that’s a yes? And this report contains all the tests you carried out on those exhibits?
AM: For every exhibit, I carried out a test which is detailed in the report; and the findings thereof. 
EK: So, Mr Mubiru, it would be fair to say that this report is conclusive and you have nothing to add, subtract or remove?
AM: My Lord, the report is as per the findings, with my inferences and opinions therein. 
EK: Is this report conclusive and do you have anything to add or not?
Judge Muwata to Mr Mubiru: You refer to the question you’ve been asked, not which one you decide. 
AM: My Lord, the report has findings on the tests that I conducted 
EK insists: is it conclusive?
AM still tries to skirt the question: the tests are conclusive 
EK digs in some more: so, is this a conclusive report?
AM: The report is to the end that I have an opinion based on the data I have. 
Judge: the report is….
AM: the report contains….EK cuts him off: the report is conclusive?
AM: the report contains my opinion based on the data
EK: is there anything you have to add or subtract from your report?
AM: My Lord, the report has an opinion 
EK: do you have anything to add or subtract from the report? (Yes/No). Please answer what you’re being asked
AM: My Lord, my opinion is in the report
EK wasn’t letting him get away with it. He asked again: so, do you have anything to add or subtract? 
AM: it depends. If the circumstances change, I can change my opinion 
EK: Okay, so you’re not bound by this report?
AM: I’m bound by the report as per the circumstances under which I examined the exhibits. 

This tap dance set the tone with which an, at times, bare knuckles cross examination that spread across two months was conducted.
